title: The Fathers on Ephesians
rules: Larry Sanger's rules for Deep Dive Bible commentary editions (emails of 8 and 9 Nov 2026): comments of at most 6 adjacent verses (Selected at most 3); cuts marked with an ellipsis; square brackets for editorial additions only; paragraphs added; one-sentence capsule no longer than 40% of the comment. Every word outside brackets is Via Patrum's published translation, checked by script.
scope: Church Fathers (all died by 749) in works published on viapatrum.org as of 9 Nov 2026.

comments.capsule: Paul's saying he is an apostle through the will of God, not from it, may be loose use of prepositions or may show that God's will serves the one who rules.
comments.comment: … we must ask how Paul is an apostle of Christ Jesus not “from” the will of God but “through” the will of God. One person will say that Paul is not everywhere precise about the special force of prepositions, and that he behaves the same way with other meanings. Another, knowing the difference between “through God” and “through the will of God,” will say it would have been absurd if it had been written “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through God”; but if God’s will is a servant while the one who uses it is the governing agent, that would not be unreasonable.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The words "who are" suggest that those who share in the One who is become beings, called from not-being into being, and the being is lost if they credit themselves with the cause of it.
comments.comment: only in Ephesians do we find lying there the phrase “to the saints who are.” And we ask, if “who are” is not redundant when added to “to the saints,” what it can mean. See, then, whether—just as in Exodus the one who speaks to Moses names his own name “the One who is”—so those who share in the One who is become “beings,” called as if from not-being into being. For God chose the things that are not, says the same Paul, in order to abolish the things that are. And someone will ask how he abolishes the things that are; but let us hear him adding “so that no flesh may boast before God.” For if someone who has shared in being, forgetting the share, credits himself with the cause of being and does not bring all thanksgiving up to the one who, from not-being, gifted him being like God and according to the image, then the “being” is abolished.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the unusual phrase "the saints who are" in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The blessings promised in the law were spiritual too, as the hard lives of the prophets show, so "spiritual" does not set Paul's blessing against the law.
comments.comment: Someone will say that because of the blessings in Leviticus and Deuteronomy, and wherever else in Scripture such things are recorded, the spiritual blessing is spoken by way of contrast with those, as if the God and Father of Jesus Christ blesses us not in a bodily blessing like those, but in a spiritual one. And the heterodox will take it that way, thinking they would also gain from such a reading a pretext for cutting apart the Godhead. But we, having shown that even under the law the blessings, if understood bodily, were not given to those entrusted with the law and who had lived soundly, will prove that those who have supposed this either make the giver of the blessings a liar, or that what was promised to those who lived as he commanded is not what the ready surface reading understands. For it follows, if the law is spiritual, that the blessings in it are spiritual too. The prophets, for example, have not obtained the blessings bodily: people who went about in sheepskins and goatskins, lacking, oppressed, mistreated, wandering in deserts and mountains and caves and the holes of the earth, did not lend to many nations, nor were they blessed in city or field; nor were their storehouses blessed, which they never even owned in the first place.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The blessing is spiritual, it is in the heavenly places, and it is in Christ, and it is already given, not merely promised.
comments.comment: Not only is every blessing with which Paul and those like him have been blessed spiritual, and none of them bodily, but it is also in the heavenly places. For it was fitting for those whose commonwealth is in heaven, who store up treasure in heaven and keep their heart where their treasure is, also to obtain the spiritual blessings in the heavenly places. How God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ has already blessed us in every spiritual blessing and in the heavenly places is worth examining; for it does not say “who will bless” us. And see whether “in the heavenly places” can stand for “in the intelligible things and outside the senses”; for in that way someone also stores treasure in heaven and no longer keeps the heart on earth—that is, in material and bodily things—but in heaven, always conversing with intelligible nature. And for us to see more precisely, both things are said about the blessing: that it is spiritual and that it is in the heavenly places; and besides these, that it is in Christ, as in the Word and the Wisdom and the Truth and the Power.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the three marks Paul gives the blessing: spiritual, heavenly, and in Christ.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Being holy and blameless before God seems to conflict with the saying that no living thing is justified before him, but that saying may mean that no one is justified wholly and for his whole life.
comments.comment: [One may ask] whether the prophetic word contradicts this when it says, “No living thing will be justified before you.” And if before God no living thing will be justified, how will they be holy before him? For if they will be holy and blameless, they will also be justified. Fleeing to the ambiguity of the prophetic word, someone will say that “no living thing is justified before God” means something like this: not wholly and for the whole of his time will anyone be justified before God, because he has certainly sinned at some point; and if that is so, it does not prevent some from being holy and blameless before him, having become such by correction; or else, if not every living thing, still some are justified.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "Before the foundation of the world" means before the world's coming-to-be, and Paul and those with him were chosen then so that they might help those called.
comments.comment: Again: 'Just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world' (Ephesians 1:4). By 'foundation of the world' he means his coming-to-be. And Paul and those with him were chosen before the foundation of the world, and this election has become theirs from then until now, so that they might be sent out together with those who have been called and might be able to help them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The word "adoption" shows that we are not sons of God by nature as the Savior is, but receive the spirit of adoption when we receive the Son.
comments.comment: The name “adoption” shows that those predestined by him are not sons of God by nature; the name of adoption would not be ranked of the Savior, but of those who, having received the spirit of slavery unto fear and then put fear away, become worthy of freedom and of hearing “I no longer call you slaves,” and who for that reason receive the spirit of adoption. And when someone receives the Son whom he did not have before, then the spirit of adoption has also made room; for thus adoption enters us through Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says "adoption" and not simply "sons".
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "Good pleasure" speaks of what seems good, and God's will was well pleased that the glory of his grace toward the saved should be praised.
comments.comment: Still, good pleasure shows the “well” and the “seeming,” so that it would not be said of things that seem to us not good, but only of things that seem praiseworthily. So we must ask how, having predestined in love for adoption those whom God predestined, he predestined according to the good pleasure of his will; and we must find a demonstration that there is good pleasure of his will upon these; for his will was also well pleased that the glory of his grace toward the saved should be praised.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Predestination and purpose may differ, with predestination first in God's thoughts and purpose following when those predestined take substance.
comments.comment: Notice also whether “predestination” and “purpose” differ, so that purpose comes after predestination: as if predestination occurs according to God’s thoughts, and according to the same, when those he predestined somehow take substance, the purpose about them follows and the predestination comes into work; hence first is written “in love having predestined us for adoption,” and second “according to his good pleasure which he purposed in him.”
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Savior is called "Beloved" because all love what is conceived of him, such as wisdom, truth and righteousness, whether they miss the mark or hit it.
comments.comment: the Savior is called “Beloved” simply; for even if people wander about grasping righteousness and truth and wisdom, still all would confess that they “love” wisdom and truth and righteousness. For this reason the Only-begotten of God is called “Beloved,” since all love the things conceived of him, whether they miss the mark or hit it—just as all are struck with awe at God, yet those who fall away from the sound notion about God go astray.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ is called "the Beloved".
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Redemption is the buying back of captives from their enemies, and Christ gave his own blood as the ransom, after which forgiveness of trespasses follows.
comments.comment: Redemption—or ransoming—happens for captives who have come under enemies. We have come under the enemies: the ruler of this age and the wicked powers under him; and for that reason we needed redemption and the one who buys us out, so that he might receive us back after we had been estranged from him. So the Savior gave his own blood as the ransom for us; therefore we have the redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of trespasses. Forgiveness of trespasses follows redemption; before someone is redeemed, forgiveness of trespasses cannot happen for him. First, then, we must be redeemed and no longer be under the one who took us captive and holds us, so that, freed and outside his hands (so to speak), we may for our benefit be able to receive forgiveness of trespasses and, healed from the wounds of sin, act according to piety and the remaining virtues.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what "redemption through his blood" means and why forgiveness follows it.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Whoever knows he is saved by grace sees how much he owes the master, and grace is empty toward anyone who falls short.
comments.comment: The one who has understood what it is to be saved by grace and not from works, and who compares trespass with trespass, would see, according to the parable that speaks of the five hundred and the fifty denarii, who ought to confess more favors to the master who remitted the debt. … If someone falls short, grace becomes as it were empty toward him; but if he does what is from himself without omission, he may say the apostolic word: “his grace toward me was not empty.”
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Someone may stumble at "all wisdom and insight", since a person in the body knows only in part, so the mystery is not made known in all wisdom.
comments.comment: But it is likely that someone, despairing that one still wearing this body can already be in all wisdom and insight, and hearing also “we know in part and we prophesy in part,” will stumble at “making known to us the mystery of his will in all wisdom and insight,” as said more generously than truly. For even if the mystery of God is made known to Paul and those like him in wisdom, it is not made known in all wisdom to one who knows all things in part and prophesies in part.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Knowing the mystery of his will in this body needs God's wisdom, and the mystery is God's hidden kindness toward those who fear him.
comments.comment: For that we may be able to know the mystery of his will and have strength to contain it while wearing a body of humiliation, we need the stewardship of all God’s wisdom. And if the name “mysteries” is taken for divine and secret things not fit to reach many, clearly the mystery also concerns those who will be saved by God’s will; for the great throng of God’s kindness is hidden for those who fear him, as David says: “How great is the throng of your kindness, Lord, which you hid for those who fear you.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul's "mystery" is and why we need God's wisdom to know it.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The fullness of the times is like the time when an heir comes of age to receive his father's estate, and belongs to the one who has advanced to where he can receive what God purposed.
comments.comment: One must also examine what the fullness of the times is; beside it lies “the fullness of time” in the same Paul: “when the fullness of time came, God sent forth his Son.” And just as the time for the heir to receive the paternal estate when he has come to a man’s age might somehow be named the fullness of his time or of his season, so in the fullness of the times would be the one who, through the roads and advances that lead to perfection, has arrived at being able to receive what God predestined and purposed for the saints.
comments.selected_reason: Explains "the fullness of the times" with the picture of an heir coming of age.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "Summing up" is a banker's term for accounts totalled into one head, so all the accounts of heaven and earth are gathered into one in Christ.
comments.comment: the name “summing up” (ἀνακεφαλαίωσις) is used of bankers’ and similar accounts that are totalled and gathered into one head of gifts and expenses or receipts; from which I think the apostle also used the word here. For there being many accounts of the stewardship of things in heaven and of the administration of things on earth, all of them, as parts of one whole world, breathing together and nodding toward one result—there is a summing-up in Christ. For not only the piecings of what is stewarded and the several accounts of what is administered are in God’s Word and his Wisdom, but also the summing-up and (as one might say) the gathering-under-one-head of all. “Head” is often also the encompassing thought; “a head,” it says, “upon the things said,” and “heading many things in few.” And “head” is so called, I think, because our head has in it all our sense-organs of life as in a summary.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the word "sum up" through the picture of totalled accounts.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: When God was pleased to sum up all things in Christ, human nature was brought back to its ancient beauty, and we received back through grace the Spirit that sin had driven out.
comments.comment: For “he breathed into his face a breath of life” (Genesis 2:7); for what truly gives life is the Spirit of life, that is, of Christ. But since he slipped from deceit into sin, the Spirit was removed. When God and Father was pleased “to recapitulate all things in Christ” (Ephesians 1:10) and to bring human nature back up into its ancient beauty, we received back through grace what the intrusion of sin had damaged in us. For Christ breathed into us after the resurrection, renewing us into the ancient beauty: “Receive,” (John 20:22) he says, “holy Spirit.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the summing up of all things in Christ gives us.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God does all things with counsel, and Paul sets counsel before will to show how carefully God works.
comments.comment: whatever God works and does and completes, he works all these according to the counsel proper to his will; for there is nothing that can make him do anything contrary to the counsel of his will, since he rules and governs the whole. And so that Paul may present how carefully God’s workings happen according to his will, he set counsel before will. For God above all does all things with counsel. Therefore he works all things according to the counsel of his will.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says "the counsel of his will".
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul repeats "in whom" out of love for Jesus, and hearing the word of truth is more than hearing the preaching, since Paul's word differs from his preaching.
comments.comment: Someone before us used to say that from much love toward Jesus Paul mentions him most continually and as it were redundantly, as one can also see in “in which also having believed” according to the “in which.” … And it is very fitting for the Ephesians, who have shared in secret words with Paul as guide, to hear “in which you also, having heard the word of truth.” For I do not think that those who have heard only the preaching, and have not received the words of the realities in narrative and clear unfolding, hear the word of truth. For the word differs from the preaching, as Paul also teaches elsewhere when he says, “and my word and my preaching were not in persuasive words of wisdom but in demonstration of Spirit and power”; and there too one must note that he says his word is other than his preaching.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the repeated "in whom" and what the "word of truth" is.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Only the one who has both heard the word of truth and believed is sealed, and the spirit of promise is the Spirit in whom the promise is already present.
comments.comment: And everyone who has heard the word of truth, which is the gospel of the hearer’s salvation, and has believed, is sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise; so that if one heard but did not believe, one would not be sealed. … I think, then, that just as the Holy Spirit, when it comes upon someone, makes holy, and the spirit of wisdom makes wise, and the spirit of understanding makes understanding, so also the spirit of promise is somehow already in the promise.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who is sealed and what "Spirit of promise" means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The earnest of the inheritance is a deposit given in proportion to the whole, so it shows how great the inheritance is.
comments.comment: … Better to understand that, just as with those who buy something and give an earnest the earnest is given in proportion to the quantity of the whole silver, so according to the proportion of the goods each holy one is foreknown to receive, the earnest of the inheritance is given, so that from the earnest one able to discern differences of earnest-power and earnest could already declare a greater or lesser inheritance laid up for Christ’s fellow-heirs.
comments.selected_reason: Explains "earnest" as a deposit given in proportion to the whole price.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The inheritance lies in the heir's own mind and soul.
comments.comment: [The inheritance is not outside the heir, but in the] mind of the one who inherits and in his soul; for nothing outside can be compared with the perfection of a mind contemplating the beauties of Wisdom and Word of God and Truth.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Spirit is now given as the earnest so that we may be fitted for the praise of God's glory, not because God needs praise but because those who contemplate his glory gain the greatest goods.
comments.comment: This Holy Spirit of promise, which is the earnest of our inheritance, is given for the present to the saints so that they may be redeemed and acquired for God, being fitted unto the praise of God’s glory. And “unto the praise of his glory,” beside what has been explained, can also mean this: “each one, for the sake of praising God’s glory, now receiving the Spirit of promise as earnest of the inheritance, and later the inheritance itself”—not, however (as someone might suspect from the wording), as if God needed those who praise his glory, but as if the greatest goods accrue to those who have contemplated what is praiseworthy in God’s glory and cannot keep silent about it, but are always becoming people who rejoice in hymning it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains "to the praise of his glory" and denies that God needs our praise.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The spirit of wisdom makes wise and the spirit of revelation lifts the veil, so the unwise and the veiled have not received them.
comments.comment: The spirit of wisdom, then, makes wise, and the spirit of revelation takes the veil from the heart, so that with unveiled face reflecting the Lord’s glory one is transformed into the same image from glory to glory. So no one who is not wise has a spirit of wisdom, and none of those who, when Moses is read, still have a veil on the heart have already received the spirit of revelation …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the "spirit of wisdom and revelation" does.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Scripture calls God's essence "glory" so that we worship rather than demand an account of what cannot be touched or attained.
comments.comment: Scripture often calls God's very essence "glory." Since that essence is untouchable and unattainable, Scripture named it "glory" so that you may not demand an account but worship. Ezekiel is the first to call God's essence "glory," when in visions he saw God seated and added, "This was the likeness of the glory of the Lord" (Ezekiel 1:28). Interpreting this elsewhere, God says, "I multiplied visions and was likened through the prophets" (Hosea 12:10). So the "glory" Ezekiel spoke of is what God calls "the I." And Paul says, "He is the radiance of the glory"—of what glory?—"and the exact imprint of his substance" (Hebrews 1:3). Here, then, he calls him "God of our Lord Jesus Christ" according to the flesh, but "Father of glory" according to nature.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Recognition of God is a re-knowing of what we once knew, and the enlightened eyes of the heart show the intelligible nature of our ruling faculty.
comments.comment: Besides these, one must hear “having the eyes of the heart enlightened in the knowledge of him”; for if knowledge of God and recognition (ἐπίγνωσις) of God are not the same, but the one who recognizes as it were re-knows what he once knew and had forgotten, then as many as come into recognition of God knew him long ago; therefore “all the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord.” … And “having the eyes of the heart enlightened” shows the bodiless and intelligible nature of our ruling faculty and of the true light.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The hope of God's calling is known by close attention and a quick mind, and the one given the spirit of wisdom and revelation will know what is laid up for the called.
comments.comment: God’s calling has a hope that must be known from much attention of life and quickness of mind; and his inheritance has riches of much glory in the saints in the upper places. The one to whom, according to Paul’s prayer, the spirit of wisdom and of revelation is given will himself know what is laid up for the called and will contemplate the hoped-for things, which are riches of glory according to his inheritance, which he gives to those called to this holy inheritance.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the "hope of his calling" and the "riches of the glory of his inheritance" are.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Lord is the inheritance of the saints, as the law says of the Levites, and the power needed to know this is greater than ordinary power, coming to be in believers.
comments.comment: [God as the inheritance:] And the law that says, “But the sons of Levi shall not be given a lot among their brothers, because I am their portion, says the Lord,” and elsewhere, “the Lord is their inheritance,” holds to such a sense. … So the riches of the glory of God’s inheritance come to be in the mind of the saints who will contain so much of the contemplation of God and of his Word by the surpassing greatness of God’s power toward the saints and believers. For it is not ordinary power from God that we need in order to know what is the hope of his calling and what the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, but a greatness of his power coming to be in us who believe from him, and coming according to the working of his strength that rules all things, which Paul now names “might of his strength”; and using this working of the might of his strength he worked what he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Being seated at God's right hand is not literal sitting on thrones but means being given kingship and rule, by which Christ oversees and rules the saints who are near God.
comments.comment: These things must be taken in a bodily figure, not as if certain seats or sense-perceptible thrones lie in the heavens on which the Father sits and the Son at the Father’s right; for thinking that way we would not say these things worthily of the divine nature. Nor is the earth bodily subject to God himself as a footstool under his feet when he sits in heaven. For how can heaven be a throne, measured by his span? And the earth a footstool of his feet, itself also enclosed in his hand? For Isaiah says, “Who measured the water with his hand and the heaven with a span and all the earth with a handful?” I think, then, that being near God and far from him are intelligible: all the saints who live according to the will of the Father of all and draw near to God, while the ungodly are far from him, of whom the prophet says, “Behold, those who put themselves far from you will perish.” As, then, one has understood who is near God and who is far from him, so one must take the saints as said to be at his right and the ungodly as it were at his left, just as the Savior also says he sets the sheep on the right and the goats on the left. And “having seated at the right” is such as this: “having established and gifted him kingship and rule,” according to which he oversees and rules the saints, benefiting them and sharing himself—Jesus who became above all through the philanthropic stewardship toward all.
comments.selected_reason: Explains "seated at his right hand" without picturing a literal throne.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul adds "and in the age to come" because there are countless orders of invisible powers unknown to us, who will be named after the resurrection.
comments.comment: And every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come (Ephesians 1:21). For in this age we name thrones, rulers, dominions, authorities, powers, angels, archangels. But since there are countless orders of invisible powers unknown to us and therefore unnameable, and after the resurrection they will be known and will receive their titles from us along with that knowledge, for this reason he said, "and in the age to come."
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says "in the age to come".
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: No rule is as great as the Son's, and although Paul says all things are subjected, many still refuse the Word, so not yet are all enemies under his feet.
comments.comment: Many, then, are the things that rule and lead those who need oversight from him, and many that hold authority, and many that lord it, and many that share their own power—some in this age, some also to work in the age to come; yet none of these rules a rule as great as the Son. For all that rule need him as their ruler; and authorities will rule better when under Christ’s authority, God’s power excelling every remaining power; and even if some are led into beneficial slavery by those who lord well, those who lord must take the science of lording from the Lord of those who lord, to lord over what they lord. Hence the one who raised Christ from the dead seated him at his right in the heavenly places, above every rule and authority and power and lordship and every name named not only in this age but also in the one to come; for it is likely there are also unutterable and indescribable names named according to the arrangement of the whole, not graspable by us—some in this age, but also some in the one to come. And from where did the apostle have these names if not from the Holy Spirit that revealed them to him? And how “he subjected all things under his feet” is said must be examined, since it is plain that countless people still refuse to submit to the Word of God. For we do not yet see all things subjected; and “he must reign until he puts all enemies under his feet” shows that not yet are all enemies under his feet.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "Subjected under his feet" may refer to those who belong to the order of the subjected, and the church as Christ's body may be an instrument of the head or a body ensouled by his deity.
comments.comment: … Another, presenting the ranking by which God ranks each into some order, will say this: he subjected under his feet all things that belong to the order of those who are being subjected. … Finding the church called Christ’s body, we ask whether, as the rest of the body beside the head, one must think it an instrument of the head, or as a human body of which the head is a part, so Christ’s body is the whole church of Christ, ensouled by his deity and filled by his Spirit—or whether these things must be taken otherwise.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The church is the fullness of Christ as a king is filled with his kingdom by those who increase it and emptied of it by those who withdraw.
comments.comment: And we want to know how the church, being Christ’s body, is the fullness of him who fills all in all, and why it is not said “of him who fills all in all” but “of him who is filled.” … And to make the saying clearer, think of a king filled with the kingdom in each who increase the kingdom, and emptied of it in those who withdraw; and nothing fits Christ’s philanthropic kingship better than this king, each of those who fill it out being benefited by him rationally and perfected, who, fleeing to him, fill out his body, somehow empty when the benefited are lacking. Therefore Christ is filled in all who approach, lacking them before they come.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the church can be called the fullness of Christ.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The church is called the fullness of God because it has been filled with God, just as he fills all things in all.
comments.comment: And he gave him as head over all things to the church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all things in all (Ephesians 1:22-23). Through this he made clear that he calls the body of Christ—that is, the church—the fullness of God. Why "fullness"? Because it has been filled with God. For just as he fills all things in all, so also he fills the church, in that it is the body of Christ. So the church is the body of Christ and the fullness of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what "the fullness" means.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The Church is the body of Christ, given its soul by the Son of God, who moves the whole body and each member as a soul moves a body.
comments.comment: The divine words say that the whole Church of God is the body of Christ, given its soul by the Son of God, and that individual believers are members of this body, taken as a whole (1 Corinthians 12:27; Ephesians 1:22–23). For just as the soul gives life to the body and moves it, though the body is not by nature able to move itself with the motion of life, so the Word, moving the whole body, the Church, to what is needful and working in it, moves it and each member of those who belong to the Church; and they do nothing apart from the Word.
comments.selected_reason: Explains "his body" with the picture of a soul moving a body.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God fills all things by working in each according to its own nature, and what he himself is cannot be grasped.
comments.comment: Of him who fills all things in all. For he is in heaven, working in a heavenly way, and on earth, working in an earthly way, and in angels, in the sun, but in each according to its own nature. For Scripture speaks about God from the things we share in, not from what he himself is; that is incomprehensible.
comments.selected_reason: Explains "fills all in all" and why Scripture speaks of God this way.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Sins are death of the soul, and "trespasses" may be the beginnings of evils which, once understood, keep us from falling into the finished "sins".
comments.comment: And sins are clearly said to be death of the soul, from “and you being dead in your trespasses and your sins.” And since “trespass” is a name proper to Scripture, one must examine whether it differs from “sin,” especially since here they are woven together: “dead in your trespasses and your sins.” And we ask whether the evils already finished by us are called our “sins,” while their beginnings, not yet falls but journeying toward our falling, are “trespasses.” And perhaps for this reason Psalm 19:12 says, “Who will understand trespasses?”—because the one who understands the roots and beginnings of sins that are “trespasses” would also be able to guard himself so as not to fall under the “sins” as well.
comments.selected_reason: Explains "dead in your trespasses and sins" and how trespass differs from sin.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "World" can mean the created order or the wicked system of human beings, and Paul calls human wickedness "age" and the constitution of the universe "world".
comments.comment: "World" is used in two ways: the created order, and the wicked system of human beings. Here Paul divided the two realities, calling human wickedness and sin "age," and the constitution of the universe "world," just as he also says in Galatians: "to rescue us from the present evil age" (Galatians 1:4). He means this present age. So he named the common human rebellion and error "age," of which those who now believe in Christ were once a part.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by "the age of this world".
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: "Ruler of the air" shows the devil to be a wicked spirit of the air, not an angel from heaven, and "now at work" shows that human weakness became his power.
comments.comment:
According to the ruler of the authority of the air, the spirit now at work (Ephesians 2:2). Through this the apostle clearly shows that the devil was not an angel from heaven, but a wicked aerial spirit. Even if the Lord says, "I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven" (Luke 10:18), he is not indicating the place from which he fell. Rather, since lightning falls swiftly from above, he compared the swiftness of the devil's fall to lightning, saying: as lightning rushes swiftly from heaven, so I saw his fall as swift.

Of the one now at work. He made clear that the devil does not always have his power; rather, human weakness became his power.
comments.selected_reason: Explains "the ruler of the authority of the air".
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The flesh is not opposed to the soul, and children of wrath are like sons of hell.
comments.comment:
Doing the desires of the flesh and of the mind (Ephesians 2:3). From this it is shown that the flesh is not opposed to the soul; for it joined in agreement with sin.

And we were by nature children of wrath (Ephesians 2:3). Just as there are sons of hell, so also children of wrath.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: We became children of wrath by nature when our understanding clung to evils from youth.
comments.comment: As for “we were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest,” we do not know what those who introduce spiritual natures from the beginning will say. How can one who is by nature a son of God be said to be by nature a son of wrath? Let them answer. We think that through the body of humiliation we became children of wrath by nature when our understanding clung to evils from youth; for according to Solomon there is no one righteous on the earth who does good and does not sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul may mean by "by nature children of wrath" in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The soul is called flesh when it desires fleshly goods, and this habit became nature through mortal generation, so we were by nature children of wrath, that is, of punishment.
comments.comment: But the soul, when it still desires fleshly goods, is called flesh and resists the spirit—not by nature, but by the habit of sins. Hence it is said: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Romans 7:25). This habit has been turned into nature through the mortal generation brought about by the sin of the first human being. Therefore it is written: “And we too were once by nature children of wrath” (Ephesians 2:3), that is, of punishment, through which it came about that we serve the law of sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains "by nature children of wrath" as a habit turned into nature, with punishment as the wrath.
comments.author: Augustine of Hippo

comments.capsule: Children of wrath can change so as to no longer be so by nature.
comments.comment: Regarding being subject to wrath according to condemnation, he calls them children of wrath, as Paul says: 'And we were by nature children of wrath, as the rest' (Ephesians 2:3). These are able to change, so as to no longer be children of wrath by nature.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: "Raised and seated" may speak of what God foreknew as already done, but the one who sees Christ's kingdom as intelligible is no longer on earth and already sits with Christ in heaven.
comments.comment:
the one who takes “he raised and seated” more simply will say it is spoken according to God’s foreknowledge and predestination, as what will be already spoken of as done. But the one who contemplates Christ’s kingdom as intelligible will not hesitate to say that the person already holy, just as he is not “in flesh” even if simpler people say he is in flesh, so he is not “on earth” even if to the senses he is seen on earth. For the one in spirit is not on earth, and none of those in the heavenly places is in flesh but already in spirit.

Such dispositions, and the grasp of things so great and of such a kind, are not earthly but heavenly; all who already have their citizenship in heaven sit with Christ in the heavenly places, if indeed the kingdom of God is within us—so that in this way we have sat in the heavenly places, seated with Christ and settled with the Wisdom and the Word of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how believers can be said to be already seated in the heavenly places.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Since all human nature was in Christ trampling on death, we are said to be raised and seated with him.
comments.comment: Yet the Word who is from God the Father does not give life to a temple foreign to him, nor simply to that of someone else, but rather to his own body, through which he is also said to have died for us, so that the good of the resurrection too might be found to have truly come about for us. For the whole of human nature was in him, trampling on death; this is how we are said to have been buried with him and raised with him (Colossians 2:12), and seated with him “in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 2:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how we can be raised and seated with Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ became poor so that human nature might reach the heights, and we were raised and seated together in the heavenly places only because he clothed himself with our poor nature.
comments.comment: Rich as God, he willingly became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9) and became as we are, so that human nature, having come in Christ into the heights of divine superiority, might put away the shame of poverty. For God the Father raised us together in Christ and seated us together in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6), as it is written. But we would not have come into these things if the One who is rich as God had not clothed himself with the nature that is poor.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: What Scripture says the Son received he received in his body, the firstfruits of the Church, so the whole lump was raised and seated with him.
comments.comment: So whatever Scripture says the Son received, it says because of his body, which body is the firstfruits of the Church. For “Christ is the firstfruits” (1 Corinthians 15:20). So when the firstfruits received the name that is above every name, the lump was also raised with him by power and seated together with him, according to what is said: “And he raised us together and seated us together” (Ephesians 2:6).
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra
comments.work: On the Incarnation and against the Arians

comments.capsule: Jesus appeared at the consummation of the ages yet Paul speaks of coming ages, so the present age may be the last month of a year of ages, after which other ages begin in which God shows the riches of his grace.
comments.comment: Often it came upon me to wonder, comparing two apostolic sayings, how it is the 'consummation of the ages,' at which Jesus 'has been manifested for the annulling of sins' — if ages are to come after this one. The sayings run thus: in Hebrews, 'But now once, at the consummation of the ages, he has been manifested, for the annulling of sins through his sacrifice'; in Ephesians, 'that in the coming ages he might show the exceeding riches of his grace in kindness toward us.' (Ephesians 2:7) Pondering such greatness, I suppose that, as the last month is the consummation of the year — after which another month's beginning sets in — so perhaps, with many ages completing, as it were, a year of ages, the present age is the consummation, after which certain coming ages shall set in, whose beginning is the coming age — and in those coming ages God shall display the riches 'of his grace in kindness' …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what "the coming ages" may mean beside "the consummation of the ages".
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To create is to make something one's own possession.
comments.comment: Since he said "created," he says: creation means making something one's own possession. And he added "for good works" so that from now on you may build yourself up.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul's words "alienated from the commonwealth of Israel" imply that believers are no longer so, since all who live by the spiritual law are kin to Israel's polity.
comments.comment:
against those who think that believers in Christ do not live Israel’s polity but some other new one with nothing in common with that, there is a fine observation here. “For you were,” he says, “at that time without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel”—as if now they are no longer without Christ, nor alienated from Israel’s polity. For all who understand the spiritual law and live by it are made kin to Israel’s polity, and more so than the bodily Jews. It follows that the one without Christ and alienated from Israel’s polity is also reckoned a stranger to the covenants of promise.

You will ask whether for this reason they are called “without God in this world”: because, as far as God’s foreknowledge goes, those to whom the letter is written were not without God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul speaks of Gentile believers as once "alienated from the commonwealth of Israel".
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We become near to God's will when cleansed by the blood of Christ.
comments.comment: “Far” and “near” are named from things spatially far or near, to show a purpose far from God and one drawing near to his will. We become near when cleansed by the blood of Christ and bought with that price.
comments.selected_reason: Explains "far" and "near" in terms of the will, and what makes us near.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul says "near", not "closer".
comments.comment: He did not say "closer" than those who believed from circumcision, but "near" (Ephesians 2:13).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Christ is Peace as he is Word and Wisdom, so we should seek him as Peace, and whoever lacks the peace lacks Christ.
comments.comment: Mark that, just as Christ is Word and Wisdom and Power and Life, so also Peace; and one must gather from all Scripture the names he is given, that we may understand him more exactly. So as the one who has him has Word when he has sought him and found him as Word (and likewise for Wisdom and righteousness), let us also seek him as Peace, that we may have him as he is Peace, and peace of all rational beings. The one who does not have the peace does not have Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains "he himself is our peace".
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The wall falls, not the fence.
comments.comment: Having destroyed the dividing wall of the fence, not the fence, but the dividing wall (Ephesians 2:14). …
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The fence is the security of the Spirit, and the dividing wall was the ban on mixing with Greeks, which guarded the Jews from idolatry until the leaven grew strong.
comments.comment: [The fence, which was not destroyed:] “I will remove its fence and it will become plunder” (Isaiah 5:5)—that is, the security of the Spirit. What then is the dividing wall? The non-mixing with the Greeks. For Jews were prevented from mixing with Greeks, so that the Jews might not fall into idolatry—they who even without this were committing idolatry. And this is what David says: “God settles the solitary in a house” (Psalm 68:6). For the leaven had to become strong, so that in this way the whole world might be leavened.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the fence and the "dividing wall" were.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Where much separates two sides a middle element joins them, so the Son, one with God and familiar to men, joins both and breaks the middle wall.
comments.comment: You find in the nature of things that when much is separated into the same, it possesses a middle element. Just as for a simple example the shell of a nut is hard and the food is watery, there lies between us something stronger than the shell and drier than the liquid, and thus they are joined; this is also seen in nuts and in streams. Since God has separated man greatly, the Son, being consubstantial [of one being] with God, possessed the human in himself, so that by the familiarity toward men and the consubstantiality toward God he might join both sides and 'break the middle wall of the partition, the enmity, in his flesh' (Ephesians 2:14), assuming the rank of a high priest.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Since the Son of God became Son of Man and stood as the common border of earth and heaven, the wall of enmity is taken away and angels and men share citizenship.
comments.comment: For since the Son of God has become Son of Man, since he who is from the Father has himself come from a virgin and stood as the common border of earth and the heavens, the dividing wall of enmity has been taken away (Ephesians 2:14), the barrier is out of the way, and citizenship is shared by angels and men, if men are willing. Those who are on earth may serve as soldiers in heaven, be below in the flesh and present above in the spirit, be with the clay by the clay, but with God by the mind.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the dividing wall is removed.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem

comments.capsule: The enmity between humans and the better powers was the dividing wall, and it was broken through the Savior's becoming human.
comments.comment: these things are said of the more divine powers and of those saved from among humans—the more divine powers being near even before, humans far (and to these the speaker will fit “having made peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in the heavens,” and will narrate the whole passage so). The better powers were in friendship with God; humans in the world were in enmity toward him; and that enmity was the dividing wall of the fence, hindering human nature from being united to the blessedness of the better. So this dividing wall of the fence, being enmity, was broken through our Savior’s becoming human, and for that reason it is said to have been broken in his flesh.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ abolished the law of the commandments by his own teachings, not as bad commandments but as a custom no longer useful, and harmful after grace.
comments.comment: He speaks of the law of the commandments that had been made customary, as from the Mosaic commandments. Having abolished it by his own decrees, among which are: “It is not what goes in that defiles a person” (Matthew 15:11)—this dissolved the rule “eat this, do not eat that”—and the not-giving of a bill of divorce—this was contrary to dismissing a wife for any cause—and “you observe days and months and seasons and years” (Galatians 4:10)—this was contrary to what Moses had given. And in general there are many such dogmatic teachings by which he abolished the law of the commandments, not the commandments as inappropriate, but the custom as no longer useful. For the commandments are honored even when they are not in force, but the law—that is, our being under the law of the commandments—was harmful after grace.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what was abolished and why.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The law of the commandments is abolished by disclosing the decrees in it, so that its letter is despised as killing and both the divine powers and believers are gathered into one new man.
comments.comment:
And notice what follows, whether it can be said more strikingly by one who interprets this way: according to the true law, of which Moses’ letter was a shadow and pattern, some were serving in the heavenly places; and that law is decrees rather than a law of commandments. The one deemed worthy to understand those decrees, once the dividing wall of the fence that walled him from the better is broken down, no longer lives by the law of the commandments. For Christ abolishes the law of the commandments in decrees, so that when the decrees shown by the law of the commandments are understood, the letter of that law of commandments is despised as killing.

So the law of the commandments, abolished by the Savior through the disclosure of the decrees in them, gathered both—I mean the more divine powers and those who believe from among humans—into one new man. The new man is understood from being renewed day by day, and he will be settled in a new world, because there will be a new heaven and a new earth.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: When the Church of Jews and Greeks was gathered with Christ as its head, he completed one corner, joining all in one building and one faith as one new man.
comments.comment: For how did the two walls not join and complete one single corner: the one being built from the Jews coming to the gospel, and the other from the Gentiles who believed? For when the Church of both Jews and Greeks was gathered, Christ having become its head, He completed one corner, with all those joined to one building in one faith, all people from the two peoples being created into one new man Eph 2:15.
comments.selected_reason: Explains "one new man" with the picture of two walls joined at a corner.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The apostles imposed only a few necessary things on the nations, so the law of commandments was abolished in teachings, in place of the many food laws and circumcision.
comments.comment: [The apostles were] writing as it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us, to impose no more burden upon you than these necessary things: to abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from sexual immorality, and from things strangled (Acts 15:28-29). For having observed many things regarding these, they prepared a way of life easy for righteousness, which also the divine apostle teaches, saying: having abolished the law of commandments in dogmas, and having again wiped out the handwriting of what is against us by the dogmas (Eph 2:15). Since the law commanded many things concerning foods, the apostles only commanded to keep away from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and instead of keeping circumcision, they opposed keeping away from sexual immorality; for circumcision, even though it was a sign and a reminder of the faith of Abraham, was also given as an evident symbol of temperance, showing how one must cut away unchastity.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Greeks and Jews are built into a new piety, and Christ killed the hostility in his flesh by ending the law that separated them.
comments.comment: For Greeks, turning away from idolatry as impiety, and Jews, turning away from the law as no longer useful, are built up into another newness of piety. “Making peace” (Ephesians 2:15). For the law does not wish there to be peace. Why? So that bodily peace may not stir up war against piety. “He reconciles both to God” (Ephesians 2:16). Since the Greeks had gone astray, and the Jews had transgressed. “Having killed the hostility in himself” (Ephesians 2:16). The thought has breadth in the brevity of the phrase. For since the law was what separated Jews from Greeks, as was said before, and the law was going to cease—and it ceased in no other way than because the Lord rose from the dead, to whom the church had to be joined as to another husband after the law—he says that in his flesh he killed that hostility by putting an end to the law.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Christ made peace and reconciled both.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: "Near" shows that the Jews had a part of piety and not the whole, so the law of Moses is not impious as idolatry is.
comments.comment: “And coming, he preached peace to you who were far off and to those who were near” (Ephesians 2:17). This shows that he does not call the law of Moses impious in the way idolatry is. For he says that the idolaters are far off, and the Jews near. And “near” shows a part of piety, not the whole. For if they had the whole, they would not be near but in it. And if again they were opposed, they would not be near but far off with the Greeks.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says the Jews were "near" and the Gentiles "far".
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Access to the Father is only through Christ, our unblemished High Priest and Mediator.
comments.comment: …the law further declared that it is abominable to offer sacrifices to God through a foreign hand as well, saying: ‘And from the hand of a foreigner you shall not offer the gifts to the Lord your God’ (Leviticus 22:25). By this it is signified in type that the Father can be approached through Christ alone. For he is our truly unblemished and great High Priest (Hebrews 4:14), the Mediator in the divine economy [God's plan of salvation] (1 Timothy 2:5). For as the inspired Paul writes: ‘In him we have gained access in the Spirit to the Father’ (Ephesians 2:18).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The Father reconciled both Greeks and Jews to himself through Christ, and through him we have access, since no one comes to the Father except through him.
comments.comment: Our guide into the mysteries [Paul] adds to this that the Father Himself reconciled us to Himself through Christ: us Greeks, who had been made His enemies by straying into the worship of many gods, and Jews, by wishing to stay fastened to the shadows of the law and not accepting the message of true worship. For through Him we have obtained access (Ephesians 2:18), and “no one comes to the Father,” as He Himself says, “except through” Him (John 14:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the "access" both peoples have, and why it is through Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "No longer strangers" answers "strangers to the covenants", and "fellow citizens" answers "alienated from the commonwealth".
comments.comment: Against the earlier “strangers to the covenants of promise,” it now says “so you are no longer strangers and sojourners”; and against “alienated from the commonwealth of Israel,” now “but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household.”
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The apostles and the prophets are one foundation of one building, so there is one God, and we should become harmonious living stones for the whole building.
comments.comment: And the words from “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets” will seem to agree with the interpretation that Israel is near and the nations far. But one must also use these sayings against those who split the Godhead and think the prophets belong to one God and the apostles to another. For if those no longer strangers and sojourners but fellow citizens of the saints and household of God are built on the foundation of apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself the cornerstone, in whom every building fitted together grows into a holy temple in the Lord—in whom the Ephesians too are built together into a dwelling of God in the Spirit—there is one God of one building and temple built on that foundation. And if the whole building fitted together grows into a holy temple in the Lord, we must make it our aim to become harmonious living stones for the whole building, that being built together we may become a dwelling for God, holding in ourselves all his theology.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why prophets and apostles are one foundation and how believers are built into the temple.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is the foundation on whom we are built into a holy temple, and the apostles and evangelists, as eyewitnesses and ministers, are foundations closer to him.
comments.comment: Christ is indeed the foundation of all and the unshakable base, who upholds all things and holds firm in well-being whatever has been set upon Him. For on Him we are all built up, a spiritual house (1 Peter 2:5), fitted together through the Spirit into a holy temple, into His dwelling place (Ephesians 2:20-22). For He dwells in our hearts through faith (Ephesians 3:17). But the apostles and evangelists may be understood as foundations nearer to Him and closer than we are, since they became eyewitnesses and ministers of the word (Luke 1:2), and became also a firm support for the faith. For when we recognize that we must follow their traditions, we shall keep our faith in Christ straight and undistorted.
comments.selected_reason: Explains "the foundation" and the place of the apostles in the temple.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sentence beginning “for this reason I, Paul” departs from the grammar one would expect, and the lines just before it show the mystery revealed to Paul.
comments.comment: I think a solecism [a slip of grammar] has occurred in the place. He ought to have said, “for this reason I, Paul, prisoner of Jesus Christ, made known the mystery,” but he says, “for this reason I, Paul, a prisoner—by revelation the mystery was made known to me.” If someone can show that both the sense and the phrasing succeed for him, that person especially should be heard. In the few words before this the careful reader can truly find a revelation of a holy mystery made known to Paul.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul's opening sentence reads awkwardly.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: As herald of the Gentiles, Paul shows that the Lord taught him by revelation, and that he measured his teaching to what they could receive.
comments.comment: Here he [Paul] wishes to show that he did not dismiss them as strangers taught by others, but that, having been chosen as herald of the Gentiles, he owed them this demonstration too, and that as the Lord taught those around John, so also he taught me by revelation. And he hinted that he could have said something deeper, but he measured his teaching to what they could receive.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: “Less than the least” may mean the same as “untimely born.”
comments.comment: …“and last of all” to Paul, as to “one untimely born” (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). Paul knew well in what sense he said, “To me, less than the least of all the saints, this grace was given” (Ephesians 3:8); and perhaps “less than the least” means the same as “untimely born.”
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Through the church in this world the angels learn great things that their own nature could not tell them.
comments.comment: …[Paul,] having written to the Ephesians: 'To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given in the Gentiles, to preach the unsearchable riches of Christ and to enlighten all, what is the economy of the mystery having been hidden from the ages in God the Creator, so that now might be known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places through the church the manifold wisdom of God' (Eph 3:8). Understand, therefore, how much the nature of the angels is lacking in knowing of itself things that are to come and in endowment; for even through this church of God in this world, which we are, they learn the great things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who learns God's manifold wisdom through the church, and how.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul’s “now” means not the time of grace but the time since the prophets began to reveal what was coming.
comments.comment: “So that it might now be made known to the rulers” (Ephesians 3:10). Reasonably so. For if it had been hidden in God, all the authorities would have been ignorant of it. For he says “now” not of the time of grace, but of the time from which the prophets began to reveal the things to come.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what “now” means in the verse.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Boldness toward God comes with a clear conscience, and its starting point is faith in Christ, who is believed in as Word, Wisdom, Truth and Righteousness.
comments.comment: …if our conscience does not condemn us, we have boldness toward God. It is a great thing not simply to have boldness, but boldness in confidence; and access again, because of firmness, in boldness. The beginning of boldness in confidence and of access is faith toward Christ. We have often said that the one who does everything by Word has believed in Christ the Word; the one who grasps Wisdom has believed in Christ the Wisdom; the one who clarifies the truth has believed in Christ the Truth; the one who lives by righteousness has believed in Christ the Righteousness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what boldness and access rest on.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul had many afflictions in contending for his converts, and “which is your glory” may refer to the boldness, the access or the faith, or to his afflictions.
comments.comment:
Contending for those being discipled to Christ, he had many things that afflicted him. So “I ask,” he says, “that you not lose heart in my afflictions for you”—the speech of one who feels himself in danger of losing heart. … Another will refer “which is your glory” either to the boldness or the access or the faith: for boldness is glory of the one who has it, access glory of the one brought near to God, and faith may be called glory of the believer.

And “therefore I ask that you not lose heart in my afflictions for you” can mean: “therefore I ask for you, that you not lose heart in my afflictions, which are your glory.” What follows will seem to agree more with this reading: “for this reason I bow my knees to the Father, that he may give you according to the riches of his glory to be strengthened with power”—for one who will not lose heart under afflictions needs to be strengthened with power.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul suffered much at Ephesus, as Acts and his own letters show, and such afflictions trouble people who see the righteous suffer while the lawless seem to prosper.
comments.comment: Otherwise mark whether what most troubles many in providence-talk is not this: when they see the holiest and most righteous meeting countless afflictions and straits, while the most lawless receive what people think goods. That Paul suffered much in Ephesus and about Asia is written also in the Acts of the Apostles, and one may learn from himself: “If according to man I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what does it profit me if the dead are not raised?” And in the second to the Corinthians: “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of our affliction that happened in Asia, that we were burdened beyond measure, above strength, so that we despaired even of life; but we ourselves had the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves but in God who raises the dead, who delivered us from so great deaths and does deliver; in whom we have hoped that he will also still deliver.” See how great his afflictions were, that he says “who delivered us from so great deaths and does deliver.”
comments.selected_reason: Shows how great Paul’s afflictions were, in his own words.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Bowing the knees symbolizes being subject to God and fallen under him.
comments.comment: …bowing the knees is a symbol of another kneeling that happens in being subject to God and having fallen under him. On this account the apostle also says that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow of heavenly and earthly and under-the-earth beings …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what bowing the knees stands for.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Kneeling is a symbol of the fallen and subjected, and the “intelligible kneeling” is each being humbling itself to God in Jesus’ name.
comments.comment: And kneeling too — when one is about to accuse his own sins before God, entreating healing and forgiveness for them — know that it is a symbol of the fallen and subjected: Paul saying, 'For this I bend my knees to the Father, from whom every family in the heavens and on earth is named.' (Ephesians 3:15) And the intelligible kneeling — so called from falling prostrate to God 'in Jesus' name,'... each being humbling itself to him — the Apostle seems to me to declare in the 'that in Jesus' name every knee bow, of heavenly and earthly and under-earthly.'
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The righteous form a heavenly family set apart as pure, and the rest of humankind an earthly one.
comments.comment: [On “every family in heaven and on earth”:] “In heaven,” he says, is the way of life of the righteous, and on earth that of all human beings. For the righteous are not stationed on earth with the living, but the generation of those devoted to God stands apart like some chosen race. And the generation of these is called heavenly as pure, while that of the rest is earthly as defiled.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the family in heaven and the family on earth are.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: “His glory” means his divinity, in which God is rich.
comments.comment: His divinity seems especially to be named “his glory” according to Scripture. And he is rich in a divinity that is great and hard to grasp …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God shares the wealth of his glory by strengthening us through his Spirit, settling Christ in the inner man, the ruling part, where he dwells through faith.
comments.comment:
…Sharing from this wealth of divinity and of his glory with those he judges ought to share power and might, he strengthens with power through his Spirit; and he strengthens by settling Christ into the inner man who can hold him.

And the most paradoxical thing: Christ, being whole and living by himself, also dwells in those who share in him; and he dwells through faith into the inner man—that is, the ruling part—for he adds “in your hearts.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the “inner man” and Christ dwelling in the heart mean.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is settled in those rooted and grounded in love of God and neighbor, like plants rooted and a building founded in love.
comments.comment: And to those rooted and grounded in love toward God—clearly with all the soul and all the heart and all the strength and all the mind—and in love toward the neighbor, Christ is settled. And as plants those rooted in love are rooted in it; and as a building they are founded in love. The same Paul said, “You are God’s field, God’s building.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains the two pictures in “rooted and grounded”.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The words “rooted and grounded in love” sit awkwardly in Paul’s sentence, and moving the word “that” restores the sense.
comments.comment:
…the sequel seems to me clearly spoken with a solecism as to phrasing. For after “that he may give you” the sequel should have been “to those rooted and grounded,” so that it would run: that he may give you, rooted and grounded in love, according to the riches of his glory to be strengthened with power through his Spirit, so that Christ may dwell through faith in the inner man—in the inner man, I mean according to your hearts, that is, the ruling parts.

Anyone wanting to restore the place without solecism, see whether he will not force the phrasing by restoring it thus: for this reason I bow my knees to the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, that he may give you according to the riches of his glory to be strengthened with power through his Spirit, that Christ may dwell through faith in the inner man, in your hearts, that rooted and grounded you may be strong to grasp with all the saints what is the breadth and length and so on. So on this reading one must move the “that” from “that you may be strong” onto “that rooted and grounded in love you may be strong to grasp.”
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The cross of Christ has breadth, length, depth and height, and the one crucified with Christ and stretching with him grasps them.
comments.comment: It is a task to see of what the breadth is now said, and of what the length, and of what the depth, and of what the height. The cross of Christ has all these, through which ascending on high he led captivity captive, and descending to the lower parts of the earth—for it had both height and depth—and if he himself ran through all the earth, reaching its breadth and length. And the one crucified with Christ and stretching with him grasps the breadth and length and depth and height.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the four dimensions Paul names.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Knowing Christ’s love is the saint’s work, and no one with that love can love what distracts.
comments.comment: It is also the saint’s work to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge. No one who has a love that surpasses knowledge can love any of the things that distract and drag away from the grasp concerning the knowledge that is loved beyond measure.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what knowing a love that surpasses knowledge involves.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who have the Spirit’s unity are to keep it, and love keeps it by gathering them into one body of Christ.
comments.comment: …it is said, “eager to keep the unity of the Spirit”; but to those who do not yet have the unity of the Spirit one might say “eager to arrive at the unity of the Spirit” or “to do the things of the Spirit’s unity.” The unity of the Spirit is kept when love binds those being united according to the Spirit and gathers them into one body of Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says “keep” the unity of the Spirit.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The one who shares the same mind and judgment toward the neighbor keeps the unity of the Spirit, and the gifts, ministries and workings all come from the same Spirit, Lord and God.
comments.comment: …the one fitted with the same mind and the same judgment of the Truth and the Word and the Wisdom toward the neighbor keeps the unity of the Spirit. But when we do not all say the same thing, and for that reason there are no schisms among us—when we are not eager to keep the unity of the Spirit—we cut it into many. Yet if God gives distributions of gifts, he still keeps the same Spirit; and if he grants distributions of ministries, he still guards the same Lord; and if he bestows distributions of workings, the same God remains who works all in all.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: “Lord” belongs to the Son, “one God” to the Father, and “one baptism” answers those who teach two baptisms.
comments.comment:
…because of those who confuse Father and Son, “Lord” is set of the Son and “one God” of the Father; and against the Valentinians who give two baptisms one must use the saying “one baptism.”

God is also Father of all, in that of some he is God and not Father, and of some God and Father—as if someone pointing out ten people, of whom five are sons of this man and five slaves, said, “This man is lord and father of the ten.”
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul’s “one Lord, one faith, one baptism” shows that Christ is one Son, who went down humanly into emptying and went up with the flesh above all the heavens.
comments.comment: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all. But to each one of us was given the grace according to the measure of the gift of Christ; therefore it says: Having gone up into height he led captivity captive and gave gifts to humans. Now the ‘He went up’—what is it except that he also went down into the lower parts of the earth? The one who went down is himself also the one who went up above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things.” (Ephesians 4:5–10) See again how great a word in this shows most clearly and vividly that Christ and Lord is one by an economic union of the Word brought together toward the human; for from both there is one true Son. For how is there one Lord? How one faith? Or how is baptism one? If there were two sons, there would altogether be two lords, a double faith, and baptism would not be one. For into whom have we believed? Or into whose name have we been baptized? But there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism. So it is clear that there is also one Son, even if the Only-begotten is understood as having become as we are. And who at all is the one who went up into height? Or who the one who came down into the lower parts of the earth? Therefore he himself went down humanly—for he let himself down into emptying and humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—and went up with the flesh above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: “Over all” shows God’s superiority, “through all” his sufficiency toward each, and “in all” that his power reaches into everything, as the sun is over, through and in what it lights.
comments.comment: Besides this one must examine the difference of the prepositions—over, through, and in. Use a bodily image such as this: by place the sun is over all things on earth, say; by its rays it might be said to be through all; and if the power of its light also reached into the depth of each, it would be said to be in all. So also in the intelligibles we take “over all” to show superiority, “through all” the sufficiency toward each, and “in all” that God’s power reaches into all, so that none is utterly empty of him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the three little words “over, through and in” with a simple picture.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God gives grace by measure, sparing the receivers who could not hold more, and the grace is not from works but is given from faith so that faith may be adorned with works.
comments.comment: And “to each one of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” we think understood thus. God does not give the Spirit and the grace from measure—there is no limit to his greatness—yet he gives a measure, sparing the receivers, since each cannot hold more than he profitably receives. Yet since what is given is grace—and not from works, since then grace would no longer be grace—grace is given according to the measure of Christ’s gift; and even if not from works, still upon something in our power. For grace is given from faith, so that with its cooperation faith may also be adorned with works, so that the receiver of grace may say, “and his grace toward me was not in vain, but I labored so much.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul speaks of a measure of grace.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus places apostles, prophets, shepherds and teachers in the Church by careful arrangement, not by chance.
comments.comment: And this house [the church] is distinguished by Jesus, placing in the Church 'apostles, prophets, shepherds, teachers, for the equipping of the saints' (Ephesians 4:11). For it is not as it happens, but with much distinction and arrangement, so that one is placed in the rank of an apostle, another in the place of a prophet, and others to tend the flock of Christ and to exert the divine instruction for other saints who are well-disposed toward learning.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
