comments.capsule: Christ gives apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers, each by the measure of his gift, to equip the saints so that the body of Christ may be built from living stones.
comments.comment:
…These too he adds in sequence with what precedes. For if Christ is over all and through all and in all, yet to each of the saints grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift, so that some are apostles, some prophets, others evangelists, and after these pastors and, over all, teachers.

If then to be a teacher is a gift given according to the measure of Christ’s gift, clearly also a pastor who shepherds with knowledge must shepherd having a gift. And how will someone be an evangelist whose feet of the soul are not, so to speak, beautiful? And that they may become so, God must supply them beauty. But also a prophet who convicts and examines the unbeliever (for such is the prophet of the new covenant) must be thought appointed to the church from God. And if these can always be in the church, perhaps also apostles, to whom the signs of an apostle are given to work, can be found even now. There is need of apostles and prophets and the rest for the equipping of the saints, that they may be equipped according to the work of Christ’s ministry, so that the body of Christ may be built and energized from living stones.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the church has these different gifts and what they are for.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: One must aim at the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, put away infancy and every wind of teaching, and grow into Christ by speaking truth in love, as a body uses a head.
comments.comment:
…Yet one must make it one’s aim to arrive at the unity of the faith; and besides the unity of the faith, to come also into the unity of the knowledge of the Son of God.

When these have come about, putting away all infancy we shall be styled perfect men, having fully taken the measure of the stature that is in secret—which measure of stature is a measure of Christ’s fullness, all who have reached the said stature’s measure having held Christ’s fullness—when they will no longer be infants, nor because of being unmoored and doubtful about dogmas walk in an infant’s condition about them, as if carried about by a surge of the persuasive points for each falsehood and giving themselves to every wind of teaching: some people not disposed toward lying but teaching by dice-play, others deceiving with all craft and cleverness, because error uses countless methods against us.

And when the saints arrive at the said perfect man, then by having understood love, speaking truth in it, they will grow into Christ all the truth-seeds given them, using Christ as a body uses a head.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by perfect men and by being tossed about by every wind of teaching.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul’s “that we may no longer be infants” can be read as modesty on his part, or as meaning that next to the ends laid up for the saints he was still an infant.
comments.comment: Since he says “that we may no longer be infants,” we ask whether he said this by moderation, including himself though not an infant, or whether seeing how far short the one who knows in part and prophesies in part falls of perfection he truly says he is an infant. The one who says he spoke by moderation will use “when I was a child, I spoke as a child, I thought as a child; when I became a man, I put away the things of the child.” The other will answer that by comparison with the many Paul had become a man, but toward the ends laid up for the saints he was still an infant; for the prophetic word names all “children,” saying, “Behold, I and the children God has given me.”
comments.selected_reason: Asks whether Paul counts himself among the infants, and gives both answers.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul may have been carried about by every wind of teaching as a man who saw strong arguments on both sides, like a ship wrestling with winds, yet not dragged down or shipwrecked.
comments.comment: After this you will mark whether Paul by moderation says not only that he is an infant, but also tossed and carried about by every wind of teaching and the rest. Yet the one who says even this was not spoken from moderation will say that as a man he was sharp and quick to hit, and saw arguments attempted on both sides sufficient to distract and put in a surge the one who contemplates the persuasions; and for that reason, as a man, he was carried about by every wind of teaching—not dragged down or shipwrecked, but like a ship wrestling with varied winds; and he saw the opponents’ arguments, as of people teaching in dice-play, not contemptible but spoken most craftily, enough to deceive; and he hoped sometime to obtain God’s help toward putting away every distraction and speaking truth without distraction and growing in love into Christ, whom he knew as his head and the head of the whole body of the church.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The wind that carries people off can be tribulation or a deceptive word, and it moves those whose minds are on earthly things.
comments.comment: Let them become like chaff before the face of the wind. Let them become worthless. This is also said in the first Psalm: 'Not so the ungodly, not so, but like the chaff which the wind drives from the face of the earth' (Psalm 1:4). Their worthlessness shows not so much of substance as of intention; for 'those who think on earthly things' (Philippians 3:19), having become entirely of the flesh and of the members, are chaff not having a sheaf, nor a stable seat. Thus a wind briefly moves them. And this wind is able to be either tribulation or a deceptive word. For thus some are carried away by 'every wind of doctrine' (Ephesians 4:14) …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The mind is in vanity when it is set on worldly cares or on false teaching, the understanding is darkened when confused, and we must avoid both lest we be alienated from God’s life.
comments.comment:
…when the mind is either toward the things of life, misusing its power on them, or toward certain dogmas shaped as true that are not true, it is in vanity; for every worldly care is vain, and all false words that pretend to be truth. And when the understanding, which is a rational discourse, is somewhat confused, neither seeing the nature of what is said nor able to follow the varied things said, then it might reasonably be said to be darkened.

So one must neither be in the mind’s vanity nor darkened in understanding, lest we be alienated from God’s life while ignorance is in us and hardness of heart.…
comments.selected_reason: Explains what “vanity of mind” and “darkened in understanding” mean.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We must care for our mind and understanding so that the Word enlightens them, since those alienated from God’s life are alienated by causes in our own power, not by nature.
comments.comment:
Yet into all these there is danger of falling for everyone who is in the mind’s vanity and darkened in understanding; hence we must care for our mind and understanding, that the understanding may be enlightened, the darkness being loosed by the true light—which is the Word of God—and the mind, turned back from affection for vain things, may be led toward God through the word of Wisdom.

If indeed through ignorance and hardness of heart those alienated from God’s life are alienated from it by their mind having come into vanity and their understanding into darkness, they are alienated from that life not by nature but from causes arising from us out of what is in our power.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that being alienated from God’s life is not by nature but from causes in our power.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Vanity of mind is having a mind and not using it to contemplate realities but handing it over to Satan, who binds it.
comments.comment: Vanity is the madness about sights, the contemplation of things that do not even exist, and also the disordered imagination in the mind. Paul clarifies this when he says, “In the vanity of their mind, being darkened in understanding, alienated from the life of God” (Ephesians 4:17-18). See how it is called vanity of mind when someone has a mind and does not use it for the contemplation of realities, but hands it over to Satan who binds it.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Those with a bad conscience still feel pain and can be healed, but those past feeling no longer feel pain when they sin and give themselves up to licentiousness.
comments.comment: And if we want to understand “who having become past feeling gave themselves up to licentiousness,” let us compare those with a bad conscience, tormented by knowing something base in themselves, with those who with all license multiply their falls. The former have not yet become past feeling, but still feel pain; therefore it is possible, if they meet rational help, for them to be healed so as to live the time ahead blamelessly. The latter no longer feel pain when they sin; therefore, not resisting even a little and not practicing self-control, they gave themselves up to licentiousness for the work of every uncleanness in greed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what “past feeling” means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Uncleanness in greed is adultery, and in urging purity Paul says one defrauds his brother by taking a brother’s wife.
comments.comment:
And I think uncleanness in greed is adultery; for elsewhere he says this in the first to the Thessalonians, in which: “For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality; that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in holiness and honor, not in passion of desire like the nations that do not know God; that no one transgress and defraud his brother in the matter, because the Lord is an avenger concerning all these things, as we also foretold you and testified. For God did not call us to uncleanness but in holiness and honor. Therefore the one who rejects does not reject a human but God, who gives his Holy Spirit into you.”

And observe that, urging us toward purity, he says one defrauds his brother in the matter if someone takes a brother’s wife; yet the Lord is an avenger concerning all these who have been defrauded, whether brothers or also unbelievers.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To learn Christ is to learn virtue, so one who has learned and heard him will not walk in vanity, and the truth is found in Jesus alone.
comments.comment:
…to learn Christ is the same as to learn virtue, and to hear him does not differ from understanding the word of the recorded conceptions of the Son of God. So if someone has learned Christ and heard him, since he learned him as Wisdom and heard him as God’s Word, receiving what he learned and heard, he will not walk in the vanity of his mind, nor be darkened in understanding, nor alienated from God’s life.

Let us therefore learn Christ and hear him; yet one must not despair also of being taught by a divine power that subjects to our purified mind a perfect and true word about Christ, as truth is in Jesus. He taught what learning Christ and hearing and being taught is by saying “as truth is in Jesus”; for the prototype substance of the truth is in Jesus alone, who says, “I am the truth.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to learn Christ.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Read in a different order, the verse means that as truth is in Jesus, so it will be in those who have learned Christ and put off the old man.
comments.comment: And “that you put off according to the former way of life the old man,” being disconnected, see whether we can restore it thus: but you did not so learn Christ, if indeed you heard him and were taught in him to put off according to the former way of life the old man being corrupted according to the desires of deceit, as truth is in Jesus—so that the sense is: as truth is in Jesus, so it will also be in you who have learned Christ and heard him and been taught in him, having put off according to the former way of life the old man being corrupted according to the desires of deceit.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The old man is continually being corrupted by his former walk and deceitful desires, and like a body that grows old, the soul shows the wrinkle of vice until the old man is put off.
comments.comment:
…By the former walk and by deceitful desires—always sinning, never doing anything of incorruption, working only what belongs to decay—he is continually being corrupted. Those desires and that old walk drive the corruption. He is not yet wholly ruined while he still does these things; he is in the process of corruption.

God's Word does not corrupt him. It kills the old man in order to make him live. Scripture says, "I kill and I make alive"; and when he had killed them, then they sought him.

Ask next how someone grown old in vice is called an "old man." Perhaps as virtue renews and recreates, the opposite vice ages the soul, so wrinkles of oldness appear on it as on aging bodies. That is why Christ presents the church to himself in glory, without spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind. While marks of oldness remain, the wrinkle remains; when the old man is put off, everything is in full strength and every wrinkle disappears.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the “old man” and his corruption are.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul says renewal is in the spirit of your mind, so the mind has a kin spirit that renews us when the mind is cleansed.
comments.comment: …The wording does not say renewal simply in spirit or simply in mind, but in the spirit of your mind. So ask what our mind is, and what its spirit is. Hear also, "I will sing with the spirit and with the mind; I will pray with the spirit and with the mind." If many spirits exist, each akin to someone, there may be a spirit akin to our mind; when the mind is cleansed and the mist cleared, that kin spirit renews us.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The new man is worn when Christ is wholly formed in us in every deed.
comments.comment: To wear that new man, take to heart "Become imitators of me, as I also of Christ," and "I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me." When Christ is wholly formed in us in every deed, we show the new creation.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how one puts on the new man.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The “lie” to be put away is false opinion against the truth, and putting it away takes testing everything and holding what is good.
comments.comment: The simple hear only a moral rule. We take "lie" as what stands against truth—false opinion opposite the truth spoken fittingly to the neighbor. Saving truth stands against that lie of false opinions. To put the lie away is no small work: one must be an approved money-changer, test everything, hold what is good, and abstain from every form of evil. Paul takes "speak truth each with his neighbor" from Zechariah.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that “the lie” means more than a moral rule.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: “Be angry” means either the involuntary first stir of anger, which even the mature feel, or assent that punishing is right, which Paul commands us to put away.
comments.comment: …"Be angry and do not sin" comes from Psalm 4. "Be angry" has two senses. One is involuntary—the pre-passion even the mature may feel when circumstances provoke anger. The other is assent that it is right to punish the person one thinks has wronged you; that assent is in our power, and the apostle commands us to put it away. So the first sense of the verse means: even if anger once entered, leave it without effect.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the apparent contradiction in “Be angry and do not sin”.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The visible sun would make an absurd rule, so the true sun is meant.
comments.comment: …"Let the sun not set on your provocation." If this meant the visible sun, we would only sin when we keep anger past sunset—which is absurd. Better to hear the true sun, which sets on wicked prophets …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The true sun sets on every sinner, so we must not act in anger.
comments.comment: Just as the sun sets on your prophets at midday, it sets on every sinner and no longer grants its rising while they keep sinning. Paul therefore orders us not to act in anger so that this sun sets on us and night fills our souls.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We give the devil room when our governing part is empty of holy teaching, faith and discerning thoughts, as Judas shows, for resisting the first cast would have left Satan no later place.
comments.comment: … [Ecclesiastes says:] if a ruling spirit rises over you, do not leave your place, for healing stops a great sin. We give the devil—or that ruling spirit—room when the governing part is empty of holy teaching, saving faith, and discerning thoughts that counsel what is best. As with Zechariah, Satan camps on the soul's regions; assents to worse things invite him in. Judas shows the pattern: first the devil cast betrayal into his heart; later, after the morsel, Satan entered. Had Judas resisted the first cast, Satan would have found no later place.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to give the devil a place.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The devil turns away from the one who guards against giving him a place, but Judas, who did not guard himself, was entered whole by Satan.
comments.comment: The evil devil turns away from everyone guarding the command: 'Do not give place to the devil' (Eph 4:27). Judas, therefore, since he did not guard himself to provide a place for him, did not turn away from him, but rather, having first cast into his heart impious thoughts, Satan entered into him the whole of Judas and worked his evils, so that Judas would feel and know that the evil one was acting in concert with him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Trade among believers often hides theft under the excuse of necessities, and “working the good” means just provision.
comments.comment: …Even among those thought believers—clean, it seems, of idolatry and fornication—buying, selling, and trade often hide theft under the excuse of getting necessities. So Paul does not shrink from rebuking thieves still at work in Ephesus. "Working the good" marks just provision: unjust gain works evil; reverent securing of necessities works the good.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul warns thieves and what “working the good” means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul wants us to give to the needy from our own labor as well as from our property.
comments.comment: …the Apostle urges us to share with those who have nothing not only from fields and revenues but also from the work of our hands. “Working,” he says, “the good with your hands, so that you may have something to share with the one in need” (Ephesians 4:28).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul wants labor to be used for.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The good word teaches and urges virtue; the rotten word feeds vice.
comments.comment: "Let no rotten word leave your mouth, but only what is good for needed building-up, that it may give grace to hearers." The good word teaches, urges virtue, and strips vice. The rotten word feeds vice and pushes toward worse.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what a rotten word and a good word do.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Strictly the Spirit does not form the judgments that make grief, yet as far as it depends on us we grieve the Holy Spirit by doing these things.
comments.comment: "Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for a day of redemption." Strictly, grief is a passion—a fresh judgment that evil is present and one should contract. The Spirit does not form such judgments, so in that sense it is not grieved. Yet as far as it depends on us, by doing these things we grieve God's Holy Spirit; the Lord says in Ezekiel, "In all these you grieved me."
comments.selected_reason: Explains in what sense the Holy Spirit can be grieved.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Sealing gives us the Spirit’s imprint while the Sealer stays undivided, and we keep the seal unbroken until the day of redemption.
comments.comment: Sealing with the Spirit gives us its imprint while the Sealer stays undivided, so we become holy—and our human spirit, and I think the soul too. God seals; the Spirit is the seal. Everyone who believes God true receives that seal from the Father, to keep it unbroken until the day of redemption and be counted among the redeemed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to be sealed with the Spirit.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Some make anger a kind of desire to punish one who seems to have wronged you, with bitterness among its forms.
comments.comment: "Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, clamor, and blasphemy be removed from you, with all malice." Some make anger a species under desire: desire to punish one who seems to have wronged you wrongly. Among its forms they place bitterness as anger hard for others to receive, or as anger that bursts out at once …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Wrath and anger differ in Scripture, bitterness is the opposite of sweetness, and clamor goes with all three, so these must be cast off in us.
comments.comment:
…Scripture often marks a difference between wrath and anger, as in "Lord, do not rebuke me in your wrath, nor discipline me in your anger." We do not define God's rebuking wrath the same way as the wrath we must cast off, nor the Lord's disciplining anger the same as ours. Speech about God is more figurative; what is named in us is plainly passion and sin.

Bitterness also appears in Jeremiah: "Your bitterness rose up before me." In Paul I take bitterness as we call people bitter rather than sweet—custom knows both. Wrath is anger starting in the soul toward someone. Anger here is not merely the genus of such feelings, but anger already primed and active to punish the one thought to have done wrong. Clamor usually rides with them: the bitter, wrathful, and angry shout and speak more noisily, pouring out words of bitterness, wrath, and anger. So clamor too must be practiced away.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between bitterness, wrath, anger and clamor.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Blasphemy is what the angry say against God or against others, and also any false word about God, since calling the true false or the false true is blasphemy.
comments.comment:
Blasphemy to be removed is, I think, what the angry often utter when, from passion, they even dare to speak against God—when every charge about anything is swept into blasphemy. People "blaspheme" when they speak evil of those they speak evil of. So after bitterness, wrath, anger, and clamor, blasphemy too must be put off.

If we also take blasphemy as every voice that speaks badly of the divine—not only from grief and anger when people are displeased, but often from ignorance of the truth, as heterodox doctrines show—then whoever calls the true word false or the false true also blasphemes, especially about God and God's matters.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul’s “all” excludes every excuse, so no bitterness, wrath or anger is allowed, including anger thought reasonable.
comments.comment: Some think anger can be reasonable, and they insert "without cause" into the gospel saying that whoever is angry with his brother is liable to judgment. Shame them with this text: "Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and blasphemy be taken from you." Here "all" covers everything: no bitterness allowed, no wrath permitted, no anger excused as reasonable. Psalm 37:8 says, as if all anger (and wrath) were sin, "Cease from anger and forsake wrath." So it is never right to be angry with anyone. Labor to strip not only all bitterness, wrath, anger, and blasphemy, but these together with all malice—malice as the habit opposite virtue, or as wickedness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the force of the word “all” in Paul’s list.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Kindness is the opposite of bitterness, and in forgiving we do ourselves good, since we grant ourselves what God granted in Christ when we receive and imitate it.
comments.comment:
"Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving yourselves as God in Christ also forgave you." We called the opposite of bitter "sweet"; Paul names kindness as bitterness's opposite, by a food metaphor. So "be kind to one another" means be approachable, sweet in character, and gentle. That comes when we put off raw, merciless, unsympathetic ways toward the neighbor and become tenderhearted to all—and by that we grant the greatest gifts not only to others but to ourselves.

"Forgiving yourselves" is not the same as "forgiving one another." Whatever good we do in benefiting others returns more to us—by the end and by our being under the law—than to those we seem to help. We grant ourselves what God granted us in Christ when we receive it, keep it, and imitate the Giver and his way of giving.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wording “forgiving yourselves”.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Taking “forgiving yourselves” as “forgiving one another” means forgiving those who sin against us as God in Christ forgave us, who also granted wisdom, truth and righteousness.
comments.comment: … [Another reader] will take it as equal to "forgiving one another," especially because of "as God forgave us through Christ," and will apply it to remission of sins: we must forgive those who sin against us as God forgave us. How did God in Christ forgive our sins? Because the Father, being in Christ, forgave our trespasses? And in Christ he also granted goods—if in Christ there is wisdom he granted us, and truth and righteousness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how God forgave in Christ.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Scripture calls union with a harlot fornication and names every sin of fleshly pleasure uncleanness, and shamefulness goes with each kind of licentiousness.
comments.comment:
Ephesians 5:3–4 "But fornication and all uncleanness or greed must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints, and shamefulness and foolish talk or coarse jesting, which are not proper, but rather thanksgiving." … Scripture customarily names fellowship with a harlot "fornication." Every sin in the region of fleshly tickling … is named uncleanness as a genus.

… Saints must guard against all uncleanness. Shamefulness tracks each kind of licentiousness and is akin to uncleanness: each act in that excretory region shows both the unclean and the shameful. Say this of what is against nature, not of marriage.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the words Paul uses for sexual sins in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Foolish talk and coarse jesting are the talk of those who raise laughter, and in their place Paul wants gracious, thankful speech.
comments.comment:
What of foolish talk, which must not even be named among saints? Simply, it is buffoonery and laugh-making. Yet those cut off from any wisdom and understanding may also "talk foolishly," and be foolish in their dogmas. Coarse jesting beside it fits the simple reading: ordinary speech uses it for anyone who raises laughter, from foolish talk or any other cause. That too is not proper for saints; rather thanksgiving to God in all things—or "thanksgiving" as when we call people gracious and charming.

So do not be a foolish-talker or coarse jester; be gracious and charming. …
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what foolish talk and coarse jesting are and what Paul wants instead.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul names six sins but ties loss of the inheritance to only three, because foolish talk and coarse jesting alone are not so grave.
comments.comment: Ephesians 5:5 "For this you know: every fornicator or unclean or greedy person—who is an idolater—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God." Paul forbids six sins, yet ties loss of inheritance to three: fornication, all uncleanness, and greed. If foolish talk and coarse jesting also stripped inheritance, judgment would seem harsh on our weak nature. Those too are improper, yet not so that practicing them alone casts one from Christ's and God's inheritance.
comments.selected_reason: Shows why Paul links the loss of the inheritance to some sins and not to others.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A greedy person is an idolater because he loves money and worships the images stamped on the coins.
comments.comment: The prophets often call idolatry fornication—"they fornicated after their idols"—and one may also call fornication idolatry from "by a spirit of fornication they were led astray." If the greedy person is one who gains money from where he must not, greed is idolatry: lovers of silver worship the idols stamped on their coins, loving the images with the metal. Somewhere, I think, the apostle also names love of money idolatry.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why Paul calls the greedy person an idolater.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Empty words are talk that denies punishment for the wicked, and sons of disobedience are the disobedient, whom God's wrath does reach.
comments.comment: Ephesians 5:6 "Let no one deceive you with empty words; for because of this the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience." Empty words are persuasive talk that would overturn the teaching of punishments for those who have lived badly. Such talk is deceit and empty, because God's named wrath does come on the sons of disobedience. "Sons of disobedience" means the disobedient—as if disobedience were a mother bearing children with her character. Scripture likewise speaks of sons of fornication, of death, of Gehenna, and the like.
comments.selected_reason: Explains both what the empty words are and what Paul's phrase sons of disobedience means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Partaker can be a word of honor, but fellow-partaker here means sharing in the lot of the worse.
comments.comment: Ephesians 5:7 "Therefore do not become fellow-partakers with them." Mark partaker versus fellow-partaker. Partaker may belong to the better—"God, your God, anointed you with oil of gladness beyond your partakers," and "we have become partakers of Christ"—while fellow-partaker here clearly belongs to the worse. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Since those who were once darkness have become light, no one is darkness by nature and doomed to perish.
comments.comment: Ephesians 5:8 "For you were once darkness, but now light in the Lord." If what was once darkness can change and become light, there are no natures doomed to perish. As the righteous are the world's light, the ungodly may be called darkness; the righteous, being light, will see light in light, while the unjust remain a people of darkness …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by once darkness, now light.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A soul that receives the truth becomes light by faith and must also show it in works of light.
comments.comment: Therefore the soul having received the truth, the luminous word, and it itself is made light, and it hears from Paul: 'For you were once darkness, but now light in the Lord' (Ephesians 5:8). And when the intellect receives the evangelical light, it is named light according to faith; and likewise also according to works. For 'let your light shine' (Matt 5:16), he says, 'before men, so that they may see your good works, and may glorify your Father who is in the heavens.' For it is necessary for the one having received the light of faith to come even into works of light.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms that being light in the Lord means faith that shows in works.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Goodness is benefaction, justice is fair distribution, and truth is knowledge.
comments.comment: [On "the fruit of the light is in all goodness and righteousness and truth":] Mark goodness, justice, and truth also from Christ's being righteousness. Goodness shows in benefaction; justice in distributing according to desert; truth in knowledge of the word of all things.
comments.selected_reason: Defines Paul's three fruits of light in one clear sentence each.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Proving means testing each deed and keeping what pleases God.
comments.comment: Ephesians 5:10 "Proving what is well-pleasing to the Lord." Do everything with counsel. Survey each deed by examination; as approved money-changers receive what is tested and pleasing to God, and shake off what is untested and displeasing. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the picture behind Paul's word proving.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Works of darkness are unfruitful, exposing them is a command the prophets obeyed, and what is done in secret is too shameful to name.
comments.comment:
Ephesians 5:11 "And do not share in the unfruitful works of darkness." Elsewhere he sets "fruit" on the Spirit and "work" on the flesh: "the works of the flesh are manifest… but the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace…" Here the works of darkness are unfruitful; whoever does them shares in them. "But rather also expose" belongs among the commandments—done by one who will not hear, "Hypocrite, first take the beam from your own eye." So the prophets, themselves not liable to exposure, exposed sinners.

Ephesians 5:12 "For the things they do in secret it is shameful even to speak." Which "they"? He did not say clearly unless one refers it to the sons of disobedience: what they do in secret—fornication and uncleanness—is shameful even to name.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why darkness bears no fruit and who exposes whom.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: What the light exposes turns into light, and the sleeper who wakes from the death of sin is shone on by Christ.
comments.comment:
Ephesians 5:13–14 "But all things exposed by the light are made plain; for everything made plain is light. Therefore it says, Awake, sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you." Exposed works of darkness become plain by the light as those exposed change into light. So to sleepers deadened by unfruitful dark works it is said, "Awake… and Christ will shine on you." Who says "Therefore it says"? Some think Paul quotes a prophet; others that he personifies Spirit-speech urging repentance.

Why to the same person both "Awake, sleeper" (as living) and "Rise from the dead"? Perhaps because the human spirit in him is spoken of for the better, while the soul receives sickness and death from sins: "Awake" suits the spirit; "Rise from the dead" suits the soul—"the soul that sins will die," and we nowhere find death of the spirit. Christ, true light, shines on the one raised from sleep and risen from the dead.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how exposure to light changes the sinner and what the call to wake and rise means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sinner is dead, so Paul's call to awake and arise is a call back to the life of virtue that was before the fall.
comments.comment: A resurrection occurs both according to the soul and according to the body; 'Awake, sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you' (Ephesians 5:14). Here, the one sinning is dead; for 'the soul, the one sinning, this one shall die' (Ezekiel 18:4); and: 'sin, having been completed, brings death' (James 1:15) to the one sinning. Therefore, awaken this one into the life that was before the fall; for this was the life with virtue. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Walk carefully by testing everything, and redeem the time by spending it on what is needed.
comments.comment:
Ephesians 5:15–17 "Look carefully how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil… understanding what the Lord's will is." Whoever tests each word, deed, and thought for what pleases the Lord can, by much attention, walk carefully—and such a walker is wise. Some mean well yet are not wise; so he adds "not as unwise but as wise." Wisdom watches the moral life carefully.

Redeeming the time means buying it back for yourselves while human life has evil days. Spend time on what is needed and you purchase it from sale to human wickedness. No one living for worldly cares has bought the time; only the one spending it on what is needful … buys it for the blessed life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what walking carefully and redeeming the time mean.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Redeeming the time turns evil days into good days to come.
comments.comment: By redeeming time in evil days we remake those days into good, and make them for ourselves not evil days of the present age but good days of the age to come.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Not to be foolish is to examine the Lord's will, doing it where we see it and bearing what comes by it.
comments.comment: Ephesians 5:17 "Therefore do not become foolish, but understand what the Lord's will is." Why "therefore"? Because you look carefully how you walk, not as unwise but as wise—so do not become foolish. Fools will not walk carefully or wisely. Examine the Lord's will and grasp it: where you see what to do, do it as his will; where you suffer, bear it as coming by his will.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a plain, practical meaning of understanding the Lord's will.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Drunkenness with wine brings debauchery, and there is also a wine of wrong reasoning against which stands being filled with spirit.
comments.comment: Ephesians 5:18 "And do not get drunk with wine, in which is debauchery, but be filled in spirit." Simply, debauchery sits in drunken use of wine. There is also the wine of the great song—"their wine is the wrath of dragons, and the incurable wrath of asps"—which all who are beside themselves and drunk in reasoning drink, full of debauchery. Against that wine stands the one filled with spirit, taking all of the more divine he can hold. We have often noted "spirit" without addition said of the better; so here too.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the plain sense of the command and a second, spiritual sense of wine.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Hymns belong to the study of God, psalms to right action done through the body, and spiritual songs to the study of creation.
comments.comment: Ephesians 5:19 "Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord." Hymns announce God's power and divinity; the skilled theologian lives in spiritual hymns. The one treating deeds and what must be done through our bodily instrument as a psaltery is in spiritual psalms. The one philosophizing nature—the world's order and other created things—is in spiritual songs. Sing according to that natural study and make melody according to moral exposition, truly disposed toward what is said: that is singing and making melody with the heart to the Lord.
comments.selected_reason: Distinguishes the three kinds of song Paul names.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To give thanks always for all things means thanking God even in hard circumstances, because his providence reaches everything.
comments.comment: Ephesians 5:20 "Giving thanks always for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and Father." Compare 1 Thessalonians: always rejoice, pray without ceasing, give thanks in everything. Keep this if you grasp providence that reaches even two sparrows sold for a penny, of which none falls apart from the Father. To give thanks in everything is to give thanks for all things—including hard circumstances. As one thanks God while sharing the world's beauty and seeing what was made for the rational creature, so also for particular things. Thank God and Father in the mediator of God and humans—in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how one can give thanks for all things.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Submitting to one another means serving one another in love, as the apostles and the Savior did, out of the fear of Christ.
comments.comment:
Ephesians 5:21 "Submitting to one another in the fear of Christ." This pulls down love of rule and of being first. The command is for all: "Free from all, I enslaved myself to all that I might gain all," and "Serve one another." Through love the apostles served the churches for human salvation. The Savior took a slave's form chiefly to serve the disciples—even putting water in the basin and washing their feet. Whoever understands "the one wanting to be great among you will be slave of all" submits by serving those who must be served.

A servant doing what suits those served may seem not to submit when the served, not knowing what helps them, order unfit things. Even then the one who acts for what truly helps both serves and submits to that need, because of passionless, beatifying fear according to God's word. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what mutual submission means with examples from Scripture.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Every husband and wife is to picture Christ and the church, so that he is head as Christ is, and she lives in holy submission as the church does.
comments.comment:
Ephesians 5:22–23 "Wives, submit to your own husbands as to the Lord; for the husband is head of the wife as also Christ is head of the church." This word wants every husband-and-wife pair to symbolize Christ and the church: the husband, if he orders marriage by reason, imitating Christ the church's bridegroom; the wife, if she lives with her husband as she ought, emulating the church's life with Christ. Then the husband is head of the wife as Christ is of the church. If they are not so fitted, one cannot say of them that he is head as Christ is of the church. So let each husband aim to be toward his wife as Christ toward the church, and each wife toward her husband as the church toward Christ; let him think and do Christ's things, and her the church's.

Ephesians 5:24 "But as the church submits to Christ, so also wives to husbands in everything." If wives must submit as the church to Christ, they must live holy, without passion, and without sin in that submission—just as the church does toward Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the pattern of Christ and the church behind the apostle's words to husbands and wives.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Spots and wrinkles of the soul are marks of sin and of the old self, which only the Word can remove.
comments.comment: Ephesians 5:27 "That he might present the church to himself glorious, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that she might be holy and blameless." Spots are like lentils, black marks, white patches, and warty marks on the body; remove them and a woman is more beautiful. Analogous marks arise on the soul, and only the Word can strip them so he may present his own bride spotless, without wrinkle, holy and blameless. Wrinkles signal old age: if anyone keeps traces of the old self and is not always renewed, the soul is said to be wrinkled.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the images of spot and wrinkle in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul's wording of this verse differs slightly from Genesis, as New Testament writers often do not quote the Old Testament in the same words.
comments.comment: Ephesians 5:31 "For this a man will leave father and mother, and the two will be one flesh." As elsewhere, New Testament writers often do not quote the Old in the same words. Genesis has "For this cause a man will leave his father and his mother and be joined to his wife, and the two will be one flesh"; here Paul writes "For this," drops the repeated "his," and omits "be joined to his wife."
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Obey your parents in the Lord can mean either obeying parents who are in the Lord or obeying parents as the Lord's command, and either way obedience is righteous.
comments.comment: Ephesians 6:1–3 "Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is righteous; Honor your father and mother—which is a first commandment in a promise—that it may be well with you and you may be long-lived on the earth." The line is ambiguous: either obey parents who are in the Lord, or obey parents in the Lord. Reject neither. Obey parents in the Lord—as Paul was to the Corinthians—and obey fleshly parents in the Lord when they command nothing against the Lord's purpose. Either way, obedience is righteous.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the two ways to read in the Lord and what obedience to parents requires.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul gives a command of justice to those who say the good God is not the just one.
comments.comment: … Against heterodox who split a just God from a good one: Paul gives the disciples of the so-called good a command they would assign to the other (just) God, when he says it is righteous for children to obey parents in the Lord. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul's wording of the commandment follows Exodus with small changes, and one must ask how it can be the first commandment with a promise.
comments.comment: … The wording comes from Exodus: "Honor your father and your mother… that you may become long-lived on the land the Lord your God gives you." Paul again omits a "your," changes "become long-lived" to "you will be long-lived," and drops "which the Lord your God gives you" after "on the earth." The command is fifth in the Decalogue; so ask how "which is a first commandment" is to be taken, when the first was "You shall have no other gods besides me."
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The promise attached to honoring parents is not the only promise in the Decalogue, since the second commandment also carries one.
comments.comment:
Some have read "which is the first commandment with a promise" as if the commandments before it carried no promise at all. On this one, they say, the first promise is set down: that it may go well with you, and that you may be long-lived on the land the Lord your God gives you.

They seem not to have noticed that a promise also lies on the second commandment: you shall not make yourself an idol or any likeness of what is in heaven above, or on the earth below, or in the waters under the earth; you shall not bow to them or serve them. "For I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, repaying the sins of fathers on children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and doing mercy to a thousand for those who love me and keep my ordinances." Mark that "doing mercy to a thousand for those who love me and keep my ordinances" is itself a promise.

… Anyone who still wants "first commandment with a promise" can answer that the long-life promise on the land is proper to "Honor your father and your mother," while "doing mercy to a thousand" is not proper to the ban on making an idol or any likeness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul's words first commandment with a promise need care.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The promised long life on the land is not meant only literally, and one should seek the good land God gives to those who leave spiritual Egypt.
comments.comment: Next one must ask about the promise that grants long life on the land the Lord God gives the saints. The Jews take this according to the letter; yet we see it is not always so, and the prophet says, "Woe is me, that my sojourning has been prolonged." Seek, then, the good land God gives in promise to the one who has left spiritual Egypt, crossed the large and fearful spiritual desert with all patience and endurance, and conquered the kings the Lord struck down and the mighty kings the Lord destroyed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the promise of long life on the land in a spiritual sense.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Being empowered in the Lord means strength in the Word, wisdom, truth and every aspect of Christ.
comments.comment: "For the rest, be empowered in the Lord and in the might of his strength" (Ephesians 6:10). To be empowered in the Lord is to be empowered in Word, in wisdom, in the contemplation of the truth, and in every aspect of Christ. Greatest among these is the might of strength, stronger than virtue and its forms—all of them powers, just as the vices are weakness. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what being empowered in the Lord means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's full armor is Christ himself, so to put on the armor is to put on the Lord Jesus Christ, with every piece of it a part of him.
comments.comment:
From what is written one may say that God's full armor is Christ, so "Put on the full armor of God" is the same as "Put on the Lord Jesus Christ." If the belt is truth and the breastplate righteousness, and the Savior is truth and righteousness, then the Savior is clearly the belt and the breastplate. By the same measure he himself would be the readiness of the gospel of peace, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit—which is the word of God, the living and active Word sharper than any two-edged sword.

What other full armor of God could the one who will stand against the devil's schemes even think to put on, except the virtue that is Christ? Clothed with him in all his aspects, one will be able to stand against every scheme of wickedness worked by the devil, its father.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the armor of God in one clear idea a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Wrestling against blood and flesh means ordinary human temptations, while Satan disguised as an angel of light is a harder fight.
comments.comment:
"For our wrestling is not against blood and flesh, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the world-rulers of the darkness, against the spiritual things of wickedness in the heavenly places" (Ephesians 6:12). Wrestling against blood and flesh, I think, means what he calls human temptations, when flesh desiring against the spirit summons us to do its works. It is no longer a human temptation, nor wrestling against blood and flesh, when Satan transforms himself into an angel of light and fights to make us attend to him as an angel of light—or anything like the things that come with every power, lying signs and wonders, and every deceit of injustice.

If the enemy persuades someone to receive him as Lord speaking in him "Thus says the Lord," so that the person even imagines himself a prophet of the God of all, he works that not as blood and flesh or a mere human temptation against one who has guarded himself this far. Therefore give the devil no place at all.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between ordinary temptation and the contest Paul describes.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul says this so that we do not suppose sins come from the nature of the body, when certain powers work them.
comments.comment:
Someone will say Paul speaks this way so we will not first suppose that sins thought to come from the flesh's mindset come from flesh and blood, but from certain powers working them. There are demons that work loves and love-charms, as the prophet shows: "They were led astray by a spirit of fornication." The same may be said of demons that implant wrath and anger; even the curious summon them and are said to make an anger-binding charm. When we hate, we do not hate apart from the demons that work hatred; the so-called hate-charms support that reading.

Because the apostle wants to teach that sinning does not come to us from the body's nature, he says our wrestling is not against blood and flesh but against the rulers, the authorities, and the rest. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The unseen powers are the world-rulers of the darkness around humankind and spirits that live in the air.
comments.comment: Our wrestling, then, is against authorities that are not visible and fleshly, against world-rulers of the darkness that wraps the human race, and against spirits of wickedness that inhabit the heavenly place—that is, the air. Elsewhere he said, "in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the ruler of the authority of the air, the spirit now at work in the sons of disobedience." The air poured around us seems filled with opposing powers.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly who the unseen opponents are and where they are.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To withstand in the evil day one needs the full armor, and the evil day may be this age or another contest after death.
comments.comment: "That you may be able to withstand in the evil day" (Ephesians 6:13). … whoever seeks to withstand in the evil day must have the full armor of God the apostle set out. Through it the adversary will be shamed, with nothing base to say about us—the devil, accuser of our brothers, who also deceives sinners as his own and as belonging to his portion. Another will say the present age is an evil day. A third reading, besides those two, will say the contest does not end when someone leaves this life: even the one who has conquered here is about to fight again in another evil day against opposing energies that appear.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the evil day is and why the armor is needed.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The belt of truth is worn by one who has given up the works of generation and hastens toward immortality, and the breastplate of righteousness protects the vital parts.
comments.comment:
"Stand therefore, having girded your waist with truth" (Ephesians 6:14). Luke also writes, "Let your waists be girded." We now know what the belt is: the one who has drawn in the works of generation, no longer serves them, and hastens toward immortality girds the waist.

"And having put on the breastplate of righteousness" (Ephesians 6:14). As a breastplate makes a fighter harder to wound—especially in the vital parts—so the one clothed with righteousness will not be struck like a deer hit in the liver by an arrow, will not fall into wrath or desire, and will remain pure in heart. He wears a breastplate of righteousness forged for him by God, the craftsman of all, who prepares and gives the full armor to each of the saints.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the belt and the breastplate with clear pictures.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Each piece of armor guards against a particular attack: truth against false arguments, righteousness against injustice, peace against strife, faith against unbelief, salvation for the head and the Word against hostile doctrine.
comments.comment:
Girded with truth, he will not be pulled into assenting to persuasive, sophistic arguments for the false. Clothed with righteousness, he will stay unwounded by injustice's arrows; none of them will reach him or make the one wearing righteousness unjust.

The one who has put on the fine shoes of the gospel's readiness for peace—ready, with his works prepared for departure, and so become a person of peace—will neither do anything warlike or factious nor be condemned with the unprepared. Where the shield of faith is, unbelief hostile to the human race's salvation has no room. The one who wears the helmet of salvation keeps unbroken the head of the soul, where the divine and intelligible senses are. And as a noble soldier, holding the sword of the Spirit, which is the Lord's word, he will cut down and destroy every doctrine hostile to the truth.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The feet are a power of the soul, and the traveler must be shod with readiness for peace like the Passover eaters, while the one who has arrived takes off his shoes.
comments.comment: "And having shod your feet with the readiness of the gospel of peace" (Ephesians 6:15). Notice he named a power of the soul "feet," with which we journey, walking the one who said "I am the way." Those feet must be shod with the gospel's readiness for peace. I take the Exodus shoes required of those eating the Passover, ready for the road, as symbols of these: "Eat it with your waists girded, your shoes on your feet, and your staffs in your hands; eat it in haste; it is the Lord's Passover." Readiness includes both hasty eating and eating while shod, so that strengthened by the food they can travel. The one still journeying must be shod; the one who has reached the holy land must untie: "Loose the shoe from your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground." So the one not yet an apostle must shoe the feet with the gospel's readiness for peace; the apostle no longer takes shoes for a road—already perfected, standing and walking on holy ground, living in Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the shoes of readiness with the Passover picture.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The evil one's flaming arrows are evil thoughts, and the shield of faith quenches them before they can enter the heart.
comments.comment: "In all things taking up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to quench all the flaming arrows of the evil one" (Ephesians 6:16). … the evil one's arrows are evil thoughts. He cannot even begin to cast them into the heart when someone is covered by the shield of faith; all the flaming arrows are quenched in it. The one wearing that shield will say, "In the Lord I have trusted; how will you say to my soul, Flee to the mountains like a sparrow? For look, sinners have stretched a bow and prepared arrows for a quiver, to shoot the upright in heart in a moonless place." Since I have trusted in the Lord, how do you advise me not to stand against the bows and quivered arrows sinners aim, wanting to wound the upright in heart? Look: I have stood; I do not flee; and all the flaming arrows of the evil one will be quenched almost at once.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the flaming arrows are and how faith stops them.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sword of the Spirit is the living word of God, which works through prayer and watchfulness, and Paul modestly asks the Ephesians to pray for him.
comments.comment: … The healthy word flows from a divine spirit; the opposing word speaks from the earth. The one who is from the earth is of the earth and speaks from the earth; the one who comes from heaven is above all, and what he has seen and heard he witnesses. The word from the Spirit is a sword; that is why Paul here calls the sword of the Spirit the word of God. For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword; it penetrates as far as the division of soul and spirit, cuts and divides, and also works through prayer and petition for those who pray at every time and pray in the Spirit, according to "I will pray with the spirit." It works for those who watch in order to grow rich in God's word and persist in gaining it, so they may help others and, through prayers, work with those who help. Notice also the apostle's moderation: he asks the Ephesians for petitions on his behalf.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the word of God is called the sword of the Spirit and how prayer goes with it.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: When the mouth is opened and speech is given, the mystery of the gospel is made known with boldness, which only one with a clear heart has before God.
comments.comment: "That speech may be given me in the opening of my mouth, to make known with boldness the mystery of the gospel" (Ephesians 6:19). … when the mouth is opened after speech has been given, the mystery of the gospel is made known with boldness, no longer in proverbs and parables. The Savior says the same: "An hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in proverbs, but will announce the Father to you with boldness." Only the person whose heart does not condemn can hold a word spoken with boldness—and every such person can—because if the heart does not condemn, we have boldness toward God, and whatever we ask we receive from him. So the one who makes the mystery known with boldness is rare, because rare is the one who has boldness toward God. Who will boast of a pure heart? Who will speak boldly of being clean from sins?
comments.selected_reason: Explains what boldness in speaking the gospel means and where it comes from.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul sent Tychicus to tell the Ephesians how he lived, to give them a pattern of good conduct and to encourage them.
comments.comment: "But that you also may know my affairs, what I am doing, Tychicus the beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord will make everything known to you, whom I sent to you for this very purpose, that you may know about us and that he may encourage your hearts" (Ephesians 6:21–22). Because the apostle's whole life, every act and energy, happened by the Word of God with Christ living in him, he sends Tychicus to announce to the Ephesians the rule of his life and the order of his deeds. It was fitting that, so the Ephesians might have a pattern of good conduct, he send Tychicus for that very reason. They would also be encouraged as they learned that the best things, and those fitting an apostle, were being accomplished in Paul.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Peace and love with faith are gifts from God, peace being the calm of the soul and love reaching even to enemies.
comments.comment: "Peace to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ" (Ephesians 6:23). … if any other gift is given from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, peace is one too—among the most honored gifts, the peace that surpasses every mind, which will guard the hearts and thoughts of the saints. It is a calm and fair weather of the soul, foreign to every storm, unrest, and passion. Likewise love with faith is a gift from God and the Lord Jesus Christ: love toward God with the whole heart and what follows, and toward the neighbor as oneself. The one who has received love as a gift also shows it toward enemies, hating no one and praying for those who abuse him.
comments.selected_reason: Says what the peace and the love that Paul wishes the brothers are.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To love the Lord in incorruption is to be pure from every sin, and grace is with all who do.
comments.comment: "Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption" (Ephesians 6:24). Some have explained loving him in incorruption as being pure from the works of corruption, and they take those works as sexual intercourse—hence custom calls the pure from intercourse "incorrupt" and those who have tasted mixing "corrupted." … See whether every sin can be corruption of the soul, and complete abstinence from it incorruption. Then those who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption are those who abstain from every sin; and with all of them is the grace of God. Since there are some who love the Lord yet do not love him in incorruption, Paul says, "Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption."
comments.selected_reason: Explains what in incorruption can mean.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
